content_html:
Introduction

dfs-large1 is now in preview within the depthfirst platform. It is our most capable model to date, designed for vulnerability discovery and validation across large enterprise repositories. Built on GLM 5.2, it was post-trained inside depthfirst’s security agent harness using our RL stack, in partnership with Fireworks AI to scale training and inference.

dfs-large1 has shown consistent gains throughout our ongoing RL climb on long-horizon tasks that combine repository-level context, tool use, and executable verification. Performance continues to improve, with no clear sign of plateauing. Across our evaluations, dfs-large1 achieves best-in-class performance and establishes a new Pareto frontier for our production workload.

To measure progress, we constructed depthfirst-bench to reflect the complexity of real-world security audits. Tasks are sourced from vulnerabilities in large repositories, where the evidence needed to establish a finding may be distributed across multiple components or repositories. Individual tasks can also contain several vulnerabilities, requiring the model to continue beyond the first plausible issue. depthfirst-bench captures the full workflow of a security audit, requiring findings to hold up under broader analysis and, where possible, executable verification. We will describe the construction and methodology of depthfirst-bench in greater detail in a future post.

In this report, we describe the multi-task RL recipe used to train dfs-large1, the audit behaviors that have emerged during training, and zero-day vulnerabilities discovered by the model.

Security Harness

Large enterprise monorepos are difficult for single-agent architectures to audit effectively. As repositories grow, audits become more expensive while code coverage and performance degrade. Our production security harness divides each repository into targeted audit scopes, giving every agent a bounded investigation surface while preserving the broader context required for vulnerability analysis. Each agent receives a bounded list of files and the corresponding scoped threat model, including attack surfaces, trust boundaries, and relevant data flows. Its shell remains rooted at the full repository, so it can inspect shared libraries, callers, dependencies, and other out-of-scope files when tracing reachability or exploitability. In multi-repository audits, related repositories are also available as supporting context. The harness executes these scopes concurrently at scale, allowing us to maximize code coverage while shortening the time required to assess the repository as a whole. dfs-large1 is optimized to operate within this framework across even the largest repositories.

Repository context is essential because vulnerability analysis is rarely local. An input that appears attacker-controlled may have been validated upstream, while a dangerous-looking sink may be unreachable from any untrusted path. Code that looks safe in isolation may also become exploitable through behavior elsewhere in the repository. Consequently, agents that reason only from local snippets can miss real vulnerabilities or report findings that do not survive broader analysis.

dfs-large1 is trained jointly on three tasks: detecting vulnerabilities in application code, detecting vulnerabilities in low-level systems code, and validating candidate findings. We include both detection and validation as learning objectives because they provide complementary learning signals. Low-level repositories often expose fuzz targets and reproducers that make defects directly testable, with a reproducible address sanitizer (ASan) report providing strong evidence of reachable memory corruption. Web application findings are harder to validate automatically because they often depend on application state and external services. Training across both combines direct verification signals from systems code with the diversity of application security tasks, while relying on the same core reasoning about attacker control and reachability.

The training recipe below targets the reasoning required for broad vulnerability discovery, rigorous validation, and end-to-end data flow analysis. It also optimizes for efficient token and tool use.

Training Recipe

dfs-large1 is post-trained with a multi-task RL recipe designed for long-horizon tasks.

Reward Design

Each completed trajectory receives a scalar task reward, which we shape before computing advantages. The adjusted reward incorporates two behavioral priors motivated by our production workload: an effort penalty that encourages efficient investigation and a report budget that discourages speculative findings.

Effort Penalty

We measure trajectory effort using a linear combination of action tokens, agent rounds, and tokens returned by tools. We then apply the following penalty as a function of effort:

Ceffort(x)=λlog⁡(1+αx)log⁡(1+α)C_{\text{effort}}(x) = \lambda \frac{\log(1 + \alpha x)}{\log(1 + \alpha)}

Here, xx represents aggregate trajectory effort, λ\lambda controls the overall penalty strength, and α\alpha controls its curvature. We choose an increasing and concave penalty function because we believe the marginal penalty for additional work should decrease as effort grows. In this manner, extra action tokens, turns, and tool output tokens for short rollouts are penalized more heavily than long investigations. This is inspired by Composer 2’s rationale, where they encourage efficiency on simpler tasks without suppressing the sustained exploitation required for more difficult tasks [1]. We use a simpler logarithmic form with one curvature parameter to make tuning simpler.

We observed that including this additive effort cost in the shaped reward increased parallel tool use while reducing or holding constant the number of agent rounds and policy action tokens. In ablations without the penalty, rounds and action tokens continued to grow indefinitely with additional RL compute.

Finding Budget

Within an agent audit scope, true vulnerabilities are typically sparse, so we apply a soft budget penalty to the number of findings returned by our detection agent:

q(n;Bt)=1max⁡(1,n−Bt+1)q(n; B_t) = \frac{1}{\max(1, n - B_t + 1)}

Here, nn is the number of reported vulnerabilities and BtB_t is the full-credit budget at training stage tt. Reports within the budget retain full credit, while additional vulnerabilities reported progressively scale it down. Our desire is to discourage speculative findings proposed by an agent without imposing a hard cap for audit scopes genuinely containing multiple vulnerabilities.

We begin training with a large budget and gradually lower it in stages, increasing pressure against over-reporting only after the policy has established baseline recall. In controlled toy runs, we found this penalty was essential to preserve data-flow reasoning; without it, the policy would devolve into reporting locally plausible vulnerabilities without establishing any reachability or exploitability evidence. As discussed below, this penalty also encouraged greater use of project harnesses to test reachability and exploitability.

Policy Optimization

We optimized dfs-large1 with a masked importance sampling objective chosen for stability under the policy mismatch introduced by our training system. Our asynchronous actor-learner pipeline overlaps rollout generation with optimization, which is essential for tasks that span roughly 100 agent turns. Synchronizing each update on the slowest trajectories would otherwise leave GPUs idle [2], [3]. The tradeoff for this speedup is policy lag, since the learner may advance several steps before consuming trajectories sampled by our actors.

A separate source of mismatch exists between rollout and training engines. Even under identical weights, differences in numerical precision, kernel implementations, etc. can produce different token probabilities [4]. In MoE models, these small numerical differences can also change which experts are selected, further amplifying this discrepancy. We mitigate this by recording the expert routes selected per generated token and replaying them in the training forward pass [5].

We correct for both sources of mismatch using a masked importance-sampling REINFORCE update presented by Periodic Labs [6]. Following this formulation, the update is:

∇θJMIS(θ)=Ey∼πθold ⁣[∑t=1∣y∣Mt⋅rt(θ)⋅A^t⋅∇θlog⁡πθ(at∣st)],rt(θ)=πθ(at∣st)πθold(at∣st),Mt=I{1−ϵl<rt(θ)<1+ϵh}\begin{gathered} \nabla_\theta J_{\mathrm{MIS}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}}\!\left[ \sum_{t=1}^{|y|} M_t \cdot r_t(\theta) \cdot \hat{A}_t \cdot \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t) \right], \\[2em] r_t(\theta) = \frac{\pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)} {\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(a_t \mid s_t)}, \qquad M_t = \mathbb{I}_{\left\{ 1 - \epsilon_l < r_t(\theta) < 1 + \epsilon_h \right\}} \end{gathered}

Empirically, masking tokens outside our trust region from the surrogate objective produced more stable asynchronous training than clipped alternatives. CISPO clips extreme importance weights while retaining every token’s gradient contribution [7], but this was less effective for our long-horizon tasks. We suspect that a substantial fraction of these p99p_{99} logprob differences reflect trainer-sampler mismatch from numerical and systems differences rather than useful policy movement. We therefore treat ratios outside the trusted interval as unreliable training signals, and we remove them from the loss calculation.

Advantage Estimation

We use Dr. GRPO to compute advantages, centering rewards within each rollout group while removing group standard deviation and response-length normalization [8]. These terms can overweight low-variance prompts and weaken negative updates on long trajectories.

In multi-task training, however, different task families can produce advantages at substantially different scales. We’ve observed that this can lead high-variance tasks to dominate the shared policy update for reasons unrelated to the quality of their learning signals. Following AgentRL [9], we apply an additional task-level normalization:

Ai,s,g,t,k=A^i,s,g,t,k−μiσi+ϵμi=1Ni∑s,g,t,kmi,s,g,t,k⋅A^i,s,g,t,k,σi=Stdev⁡({A^i,s,g,t,k:mi,s,g,t,k=1})\begin{gathered} A_{i,s,g,t,k} = \frac{\hat{A}_{i,s,g,t,k} - \mu_i}{\sigma_i + \epsilon} \\[12pt] \mu_i = \frac{1}{N_i} \sum_{s,g,t,k} m_{i,s,g,t,k} \cdot \hat{A}_{i,s,g,t,k}, \qquad \sigma_i = \operatorname{Stdev}(\{\hat{A}_{i,s,g,t,k} : m_{i,s,g,t,k} = 1\}) \end{gathered}

Context Compaction

For long-horizon rollouts, dfs-large1 reuses the summarization-based context compaction recipe introduced with dfs-mini1 [10]. As the context window fills up, the policy compresses the trajectory into a concise state summary and continues from that representation rather than the full transcript. Because the same policy generates these summaries and receives the final trajectory reward, context management becomes part of the learned agent behavior.

Results: Learned Audit Strategy

During training, we observed that dfs-large1’s audit strategy shifted from broad enumeration toward testing specific vulnerability hypotheses. In judged samples, later checkpoints spent a larger share of turns tracing attacker-controlled inputs and used executable harnesses more often, while repository reads and searches declined.

These two condensed trajectories show the shift: dfs-large1 tests critical assumptions and carries hypotheses through to executable evidence.

We suspect the finding budget, effort penalty, and joint training on vulnerability validation all contributed to this shift. The finding budget creates pressure against unsupported reports, the effort penalty rewards targeted investigation over repeated browsing, and validation training rewards turning a hypothesis into executable evidence.

Real-World Vulnerability Discovery

Beyond our evaluations, we are testing dfs-large1 across production code-scanning workflows. Separately, a previous checkpoint supported parts of our Ruby ecosystem campaign. That broader campaign validated 105 vulnerabilities across 34 projects, roughly 61% of them memory-safety issues [11]. We plan to apply dfs-large1 to more open-source security research.

Continued Training

Ultimately, our goal is to deliver the best possible agentic product experience for customers using the depthfirst security harness. That means shorter time to actionable findings, lower cost per audit, and fewer false positives.

We have collected thousands of executable security environments. We have not yet saturated these environments, leaving substantial headroom to keep scaling the training recipe, annealing our finding penalty to further reduce false positives, and improving token and turn efficiency.

Evaluation Methodology

Unless otherwise specified, all models are evaluated at high thinking difficulty and executed within depthfirst’s security harness. To preserve evaluation integrity, our sandboxes block internet access and expose only a shallow clone of each repository with depth 1 and no commit history. We also use LLM behavioral monitors to flag reward hacking, superficial pattern matching, or attempts to obtain information unavailable in the evaluation by searching the internet or inspecting future commits containing vulnerability patch information.

Finally, we reviewed every passing trajectory to verify that it reflected authentic vulnerability discovery, and we confirmed that no failures resulted from cybersecurity-safety refusals.

blocks.html_en: Large enterprise monorepos are difficult for single-agent architectures to audit effectively. As repositories grow, audits become more expensive while code coverage and performance degrade. Our production security harness divides each repository into targeted audit scopes, giving every agent a bounded investigation surface while preserving the broader context required for vulnerability analysis. Each agent receives a bounded list of files and the corresponding scoped threat model, including attack surfaces, trust boundaries, and relevant data flows. Its shell remains rooted at the full repository, so it can inspect shared libraries, callers, dependencies, and other out-of-scope files when tracing reachability or exploitability. In multi-repository audits, related repositories are also available as supporting context. The harness executes these scopes concurrently at scale, allowing us to maximize code coverage while shortening the time required to assess the repository as a whole. dfs-large1 is optimized to operate within this framework across even the largest repositories.

blocks.html_en: Repository context is essential because vulnerability analysis is rarely local. blocks.html_en: dfs-large1 is trained jointly on three tasks: detecting vulnerabilities in application code, detecting vulnerabilities in low-level systems code, and validating candidate findings. We include both detection and validation as learning objectives because they provide complementary learning signals. Low-level repositories often expose fuzz targets and reproducers that make defects directly testable, with a reproducible address sanitizer (ASan) report providing strong evidence of reachable memory corruption. Web application findings are harder to validate automatically because they often depend on application state and external services. Training across both combines direct verification signals from systems code with the diversity of application security tasks, while relying on the same core reasoning about attacker control and reachability.

content_html_zh:
介绍

dfs-large1 现已在深度优先平台中提供预览版。 它是我们迄今为止最强大的模型，专为大型企业存储库中的漏洞发现和验证而设计。 它基于 GLM 5.2 构建，使用我们的 RL 堆栈在深度优先的安全代理工具内进行后训练，并与 Fireworks AI 合作来扩展训练和推理。

dfs-large1 在我们持续的 RL 爬升过程中，结合了存储库级上下文、工具使用和可执行验证的长期任务，显示出持续的收益。 业绩持续改善，没有明显的停滞迹象。 在我们的评估中，dfs-large1 实现了一流的性能，并为我们的生产工作负载建立了新的帕累托前沿。

为了衡量进展，我们构建了深度优先基准来反映现实世界安全审计的复杂性。 任务源自大型存储库中的漏洞，其中建立发现所需的证据可能分布在多个组件或存储库中。 单个任务还可能包含多个漏洞，要求模型继续超越第一个看似合理的问题。 deepfirst-bench 捕获安全审计的完整工作流程，要求调查结果经过更广泛的分析，并在可能的情况下进行可执行验证。 我们将在以后的文章中更详细地描述深度优先平台的构造和方法。

在本报告中，我们描述了用于训练 dfs-large1 的多任务强化学习配方、训练期间出现的审计行为以及模型发现的零日漏洞。

安全线束

大型企业单一存储库很难通过单代理架构进行有效审计。 随着存储库的增长，审计变得更加昂贵，同时代码覆盖率和性能也会下降。 我们的生产安全工具将每个存储库划分为目标审计范围，为每个代理提供有限的调查范围，同时保留漏洞分析所需的更广泛的背景。 每个代理都会收到有限的文件列表和相应的范围威胁模型，包括攻击面、信任边界和相关数据流。 它的 shell 仍然植根于完整的存储库，因此它可以在跟踪可访问性或可利用性时检查共享库、调用者、依赖项和其他范围外的文件。 在多存储库审计中，相关存储库也可用作支持上下文。 该工具大规模同时执行这些范围，使我们能够最大限度地提高代码覆盖率，同时缩短评估整个存储库所需的时间。 dfs-large1 经过优化，可以在此框架内跨最大的存储库运行。

存储库上下文至关重要，因为漏洞分析很少是本地的。 看似由攻击者控制的输入可能已在上游得到验证，而看似危险的接收器可能无法从任何不受信任的路径到达。 孤立地看起来安全的代码也可能通过存储库中其他地方的行为而被利用。 因此，仅从本地片段进行推理的代理可能会错过真正的漏洞或报告无法通过更广泛分析的结果。

dfs-large1 针对三项任务进行联合训练：检测应用程序代码中的漏洞、检测低级系统代码中的漏洞以及验证候选结果。 我们将检测和验证都作为学习目标，因为它们提供了互补的学习信号。 低级存储库通常会暴露模糊目标和重现器，使缺陷可以直接测试，并通过可重现的地址清理器 (ASan) 报告提供可访问内存损坏的有力证据。 Web 应用程序的结果很难自动验证，因为它们通常依赖于应用程序状态和外部服务。 两者的训练将来自系统代码的直接验证信号与应用程序安全任务的多样性结合起来，同时依赖于关于攻击者控制和可达性的相同核心推理。

下面的培训方案针对广泛的漏洞发现、严格的验证和端到端数据流分析所需的推理。 它还优化了令牌和工具的高效使用。

训练食谱

dfs-large1 使用专为长视野任务设计的多任务 RL 配方进行后训练。

奖励设计

每个完成的轨迹都会收到一个标量任务奖励，这是我们在计算优势之前形成的。 调整后的奖励包含了由我们的生产工作量驱动的两个行为先验：鼓励有效调查的努力惩罚和阻止推测性发现的报告预算。

努力惩罚

我们使用操作标记、代理回合和工具返回的标记的线性组合来测量轨迹工作量。 然后，我们将以下惩罚作为努力的函数：

Ceffort(x)=λlog⁡(1+αx)log⁡(1+α)C_{\text{effort}}(x) = \lambda \frac{\log(1 + \alpha x)}{\log(1 + \alpha)}

这里，xx表示总轨迹努力，λ\lambda控制总体惩罚强度，α\alpha控制其曲率。 我们选择递增和凹的惩罚函数，因为我们相信额外工作的边际惩罚应该随着努力的增加而减少。 通过这种方式，短期部署的额外动作令牌、回合和工具输出令牌会比长期调查受到更严重的惩罚。 这是受到 Composer 2 基本原理的启发，它们鼓励更简单任务的效率，而不抑制更困难任务所需的持续开发 [1]。 我们使用一种更简单的对数形式和一个曲率参数来使调整更简单。

我们观察到，将这种额外的努力成本包含在成形奖励中会增加并行工具的使用，同时减少或保持代理轮数和政策行动代币的数量不变。 在没有惩罚的消融中，随着额外的 RL 计算，轮次和动作代币继续无限增长。

寻找预算

在代理审核范围内，真正的漏洞通常很少，因此我们对检测代理返回的结果数量应用软预算惩罚：

q(n;Bt)=1max⁡(1,n−Bt+1)q(n;B_t) = \frac{1}{\max(1, n - B_t + 1)}

这里，nn是报告的漏洞数量，BtB_t是训练阶段tt的全额预算。 预算内的报告保留全部信用，而报告的其他漏洞则逐渐缩小预算范围。 我们的愿望是阻止代理提出推测性结果，而不对真正包含多个漏洞的审计范围施加硬性上限。

我们开始以大量预算进行培训，然后逐步逐步降低预算，只有在政策建立基线召回后才增加防止过度报告的压力。 在受控玩具运行中，我们发现这种惩罚对于保持数据流推理至关重要；如果没有它，该政策将转变成报告当地可能存在的漏洞，而没有建立任何可达性或可利用性证据。 如下所述，这种惩罚还鼓励更多地使用项目工具来测试可达性和可利用性。

政策优化

我们优化了 dfs-large1，选择了一个掩蔽重要性采样目标，以确保在我们的训练系统引入的策略不匹配的情况下保持稳定性。 我们的异步参与者-学习者管道将推出生成与优化重叠，这对于跨越大约 100 个代理轮次的任务至关重要。 同步最慢轨迹上的每个更新否则会使 GPU 空闲 [2]、[3]。 这种加速的代价是策略滞后，因为学习者在使用我们的参与者采样的轨迹之前可能会前进几个步骤。

推出引擎和训练引擎之间存在另一个不匹配的来源。 即使在相同的权重下，数值精度、内核实现等方面的差异也可能产生不同的令牌概率 [4]。 在教育部模型中，这些微小的数字差异也会改变选择的专家，从而进一步放大这种差异。 我们通过记录每个生成的令牌选择的专家路线并在训练前向传递中重放它们来缓解这种情况[5]。

我们使用Periodic Labs [6]提出的屏蔽重要性采样增强更新来纠正这两种不匹配的来源。 按照这个公式，更新为：

∇θJMIS(θ)=Ey∼πθold ⁣[Σt=1∣y∣Mt⋅rt(θ)⋅A^t⋅∇θlog⁡πθ(at∣st)],rt(θ)=πθ(at∣st)πθold(at∣st),Mt=I{1−ϵl<rt(θ)<1+ϵh}\begin{聚集} \nabla_\theta J_{\mathrm{MIS}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}}\!\left[ \sum_{t=1}^{|y|} M_t \cdot r_t(\theta) \cdot \hat{A}_t \cdot \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t) \right], \\[2em] r_t(\theta) = \frac{\pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)} {\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(a_t \mid s_t)}, \qquad M_t = \mathbb{I}_{\left\{ 1 - \epsilon_l < r_t(\theta) < 1 + \epsilon_h \right\}} \end{聚集}

根据经验，从代理目标中屏蔽我们信任区域之外的令牌比修剪替代方案产生更稳定的异步训练。 CISPO 削减了极端重要性权重，同时保留了每个 token 的梯度贡献 [7]，但这对于我们的长期任务来说效果较差。 我们怀疑这些 p99p_{99} logprob 差异的很大一部分反映了来自数值和系统差异的训练器-采样器不匹配，而不是有用的策略运动。 因此，我们将可信区间之外的比率视为不可靠的训练信号，并将它们从损失计算中删除。

优势评估

我们使用 GRPO 博士来计算优势，将奖励集中在每个推出组内，同时消除组标准差和响应长度标准化 [8]。 这些术语可能会加重低方差提示并削弱长轨迹上的负面更新。

然而，在多任务训练中，不同的任务族可以在截然不同的规模上产生优势。 我们观察到，这可能会导致高方差任务由于与学习信号质量无关的原因而主导共享策略更新。 遵循 AgentRL [9]，我们应用了额外的任务级标准化：

Ai,s,g,t,k=A^i,s,g,t,k−μiσi+ϵμi=1NiΣs,g,t,kmi,s,g,t,k⋅A^i,s,g,t,k,σi=Stdev⁡({A^i,s,g,t,k:mi,s,g,t,k=1})\begin{聚集} A_{i,s,g,t,k} = \frac{\hat{A}_{i,s,g,t,k} - \mu_i}{\sigma_i + \epsilon} \\[12pt] \mu_i = \frac{1}{N_i} \sum_{s,g,t,k} m_{i,s,g,t,k} \cdot \hat{A}_{i,s,g,t,k}, \qquad \sigma_i = \operatorname{Stdev}(\{\hat{A}_{i,s,g,t,k} : m_{i,s,g,t,k} = 1\}) \end{聚集}

上下文压缩

对于长期部署，dfs-large1 重用 dfs-mini1 [10] 引入的基于摘要的上下文压缩方法。 当上下文窗口填满时，策略将轨迹压缩为简洁的状态摘要，并从该表示而不是完整的记录继续。 由于相同的策略生成这些摘要并接收最终的轨迹奖励，因此上下文管理成为学习代理行为的一部分。

结果：学习审计策略

在训练过程中，我们观察到 dfs-large1 的审计策略从广泛枚举转向测试特定的漏洞假设。 在判断的样本中，后来的检查点花费了更多的时间来跟踪攻击者控制的输入，并更频繁地使用可执行工具，而存储库读取和搜索则有所下降。

这两条浓缩轨迹显示了这种转变：dfs-large1 测试关键假设并将假设转化为可执行的证据。

我们怀疑发现预算、工作量惩罚和漏洞验证联合培训都促成了这一转变。 发现预算对没有支持的报告产生压力，努力惩罚奖励有针对性的调查而不是重复浏览，验证培训奖励将假设转化为可执行的证据。

现实世界的漏洞发现

除了我们的评估之外，我们还在生产代码扫描工作流程中测试 dfs-large1。 另外，之前的检查点支持我们 Ruby 生态系统活动的部分内容。 这场更广泛的活动验证了 34 个项目的 105 个漏洞，其中大约 61% 是内存安全问题 [11]。 我们计划将 dfs-large1 应用到更多开源安全研究中。

继续培训

最终，我们的目标是使用深度优先安全工具为客户提供尽可能最佳的代理产品体验。 这意味着获得可采取行动的调查结果的时间更短，每次审计的成本更低，误报更少。

我们收集了数千个可执行的安全环境。 我们还没有使这些环境饱和，留下了很大的空间来继续扩展训练方案，退火我们的发现惩罚以进一步减少误报，并提高令牌和回合效率。

评估方法

除非另有说明，所有模型都以高思维难度进行评估，并在深度优先的安全框架内执行。 为了保持评估完整性，我们的沙箱会阻止互联网访问，并仅公开每个存储库的深度为 1 且没有提交历史记录的浅层克隆。 我们还使用 LLM 行为监视器来标记奖励黑客行为、肤浅的模式匹配，或尝试通过搜索互联网或检查包含漏洞补丁信息的未来提交来获取评估中不可用的信息。

最后，我们审查了每一条经过的轨迹，以验证它是否反映了真实的漏洞发现，并确认没有因网络安全拒绝而导致失败。
